title: Compiler warnings, language standards and portability flags
learningObjectives: Explain that -std selects a language dialect on GCC- and Clang-like compilers and does not guarantee identical support across all toolchains.
Recognize common warning options such as -Wall, -Wextra, -Wpedantic and selected conversion diagnostics.
Distinguish a compiler warning from an error and understand why warnings should be investigated rather than blindly suppressed.
Use consistent documented compiler options for every translation unit and automated build.
Identify compiler extensions and implementation-defined behaviour that can reduce portability.
Build and test code with more than one supported compiler or target when portability is a project requirement.

understand.concept: C compilers offer language-standard modes and diagnostic options. On GCC- and Clang-like toolchains, -std=c17 selects a C17 language mode, while -Wall, -Wextra and -Wpedantic enable groups of diagnostics. The exact options, warning coverage and accepted language features depend on compiler and version. A warning is diagnostic evidence that code may be suspicious; it is not a formal proof of a defect or of correctness.
understand.whyItMatters: Explicit standards and warning policies make builds easier to reproduce and help detect suspicious conversions, missing declarations and nonportable extensions. Inconsistent flags between source files or between local and CI builds can hide defects or produce incompatible assumptions.
understand.analogy: Compiler flags are like a documented inspection checklist: they tell a particular tool which language rules and diagnostic categories to apply.
understand.analogyLimit: Different compilers implement different options and diagnostic sets. A warning-free build under one compiler does not prove portability or correctness on every implementation.

explain.narrative: Select a language version deliberately and document it. The spelling of standard modes varies across compilers; check the toolchain documentation instead of assuming a flag is universal. Enable useful warnings and treat each diagnostic as a question to investigate. Fix the cause when possible; do not silence a warning simply to obtain a green build.\n\nSome diagnostics are grouped options and some are individually enabled. More warnings can reveal real defects but can also produce false positives or toolchain-specific noise. Keep the policy consistent across all translation units and CI. When a project supports multiple compilers, use a documented compiler matrix and resolve differences rather than assuming identical defaults. Avoid extensions when strict ISO C portability is required, and isolate unavoidable platform-specific code behind a clear interface.

examples.title: Build a small C17 program with warnings
examples.explanation: The program is ordinary C. The commented command selects C17 and requests several diagnostic groups on GCC- and Clang-like compilers. Some flags are not portable to every compiler, so document the supported toolchain.

examples.title: Use a portable interface instead of assuming an extension
examples.explanation: stdint.h provides exact-width typedefs only when the implementation supports the corresponding type. The example uses the standard uint32_t name and an explicit conversion for the printf format. A project should still check target support and use the matching format macros from inttypes.h when printing exact-width types in a fully general way.

practise.guidedTask: Compile a small program with and without warning options. Record each diagnostic, determine whether it identifies a real risk, fix the underlying cause and explain any justified suppression.
practise.independentTask: Choose a small C program and build it with two supported compilers in the same standard mode. Compare diagnostics and behaviour, then document compiler versions, flags, portability issues and any extensions used.
hints: The standard-mode option is toolchain-specific even when its spelling is familiar.
Warnings are evidence to investigate, not proof that a program is wrong or right.
Keep compiler flags consistent across every translation unit.
Do not silence warnings without understanding and documenting the reason.
Use a second compiler or target to discover assumptions hidden by one implementation.
A successful strict build does not replace boundary, invalid-input and runtime testing.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a standard-mode option such as -std=c17?
options: Select the C language dialect accepted by the compiler
Guarantee the same executable on every computer
Automatically test every input
Enable network access
questions.answer: Select the C language dialect accepted by the compiler
questions.explanation: The option requests a language mode; it does not guarantee identical toolchain behaviour.

questions.prompt: What does -Wall commonly do on GCC- and Clang-like compilers?
options: Enable a commonly used group of warnings
Treat every warning as an error on every compiler
Disable all diagnostics
Select the C23 standard
questions.answer: Enable a commonly used group of warnings
questions.explanation: -Wall enables a warning group; its exact coverage is compiler-specific.

questions.prompt: What is a sound response to a new compiler warning?
options: Understand the diagnostic and fix the underlying cause when appropriate
Suppress it immediately without review
Assume the compiler is always wrong
Delete the test suite
questions.answer: Understand the diagnostic and fix the underlying cause when appropriate
questions.explanation: Diagnostics should be investigated; suppressions need a clear justification.

questions.prompt: Does a warning-free build prove portability to every C compiler?
options: No, diagnostics and implementation support differ
Yes, for every platform
Only if the program has comments
Yes, if the executable is small
questions.answer: No, diagnostics and implementation support differ
questions.explanation: Portability requires standards-aware code and testing on the intended implementations.

questions.prompt: Why use consistent flags for all translation units?
options: To keep language and diagnostic assumptions aligned across the program
To make every source file identical
To remove the need for headers
To prevent the linker from running
questions.answer: To keep language and diagnostic assumptions aligned across the program
questions.explanation: Different compilation settings can create inconsistent assumptions and weaken diagnostics.
